question_text: Prove that the radius of the right circular cylinder of greatest curved surface area which can be inscribed in a given cone is half of that of the cone.

steps.margin_note: First mark. The examiner looks for the similar-triangle ratio written the right way round: h/H = (R − x)/R. A wide cylinder must be short, so h must fall as x rises.

steps.why: The cone is the constraint: choosing the cylinder's radius fixes its height. Similar triangles give the link between x and h; without it the curved surface contains two variables.
common_mistakes: Writing h/H = x/R, which makes the cylinder tallest when it is widest.
Assuming the cylinder's height equals the cone's height.
steps.memory_tip: Check the ratio at the two ends: x = 0 must give h = H and x = R must give h = 0. h = H(R − x)/R does both, and it is the relation the similar triangles give.

steps.why: The curved surface of a cylinder is 2π times radius times height. Substituting h turns it into a quadratic in x, and a quadratic needs only one differentiation to locate its stationary point.
common_mistakes: Using the total surface area 2πx(x + h) instead of the curved surface 2πxh.
Treating R or H as a variable and differentiating them.
steps.memory_tip: Curved surface is the side of the cylinder only: 2π times radius times height, with no flat ends. Keep every fixed letter outside the bracket so the differentiation is short.

steps.why: The constant 2πH/R is positive and can never be zero, so the derivative is zero exactly where the bracket is zero. That reduces the work to one linear equation.
common_mistakes: Setting the constant 2πH/R to zero as well.
Differentiating Rx as 1 instead of R, and losing the R.
steps.memory_tip: A positive constant multiplying a function never moves its stationary point, so set only the bracket to zero.

steps.why: The question says prove, so the working must show the value is a maximum and not merely a stationary point. The second derivative test is that proof and carries its own mark.
common_mistakes: Stopping at x = R/2 with no test, which proves nothing about it being greatest.
Claiming the greatest VOLUME cylinder also has radius R/2 — that one has radius 2R/3.
steps.memory_tip: Greatest curved surface gives radius R/2 and height H/2. Greatest volume is a different question with a different answer, radius 2R/3.

insider_note: Use similar triangles to write the cylinder's height through its radius, so the surface area has ONE variable. The answer is half the cone's radius, independent of the height.
